Residuals are only meaningful on data the model did not fit. Training residuals shrink as capacity grows, so always compute metrics on a validation or test split, or on out-of-fold predictions from cross-validation.

Sign convention matters when you read plots and bias: with e = y - y_hat, a positive mean residual means the model under-predicts on average. For ordinary least squares with an intercept, training residuals sum to exactly zero, so mean bias only shows up on held-out data or within subgroups. Slice residuals by segment (region, price band, time period) because a model can be unbiased overall and systematically wrong for one group. For time series, also plot residuals over time: autocorrelated residuals mean the model is missing temporal structure, and random-split metrics will be optimistic.

MAE, MSE and RMSE are all scale-dependent, so only compare them on the same target in the same units. RMSE always lies between MAE and sqrt(n) x MAE: equality at the low end means every error has the same size; the high end is reached when one error carries everything.

MSE decomposes into bias^2 + variance of the errors, which is why a constant offset raises MSE even if the shape of predictions is perfect. RMSE is not an average of per-example quantities, so it does not decompose across subgroups the way MAE and MSE do: average MSE per group, then take the square root.

Interviewers often ask which metric is optimized by which prediction: the mean minimizes MSE, the median minimizes MAE. Reporting MAE for a model trained to predict the mean is legitimate but can look worse than a median-targeting model.

R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot compares your model with the constant predictor that outputs the mean of y. On training data with an OLS fit and intercept it lies in [0, 1] and equals the squared correlation between y and y_hat. On test data it can be any value up to 1, and a negative value means the model is worse than predicting the mean. Note that libraries compute SS_tot with the test-set mean, which slightly favors the baseline.

R^2 depends on the variance of the target in the evaluation set: the same model scores higher on a population with a wider range of y. That makes it unreliable for comparing datasets. Adjusted R^2 subtracts a penalty for the number of predictors p, but it is an in-sample correction; for model selection, held-out error or cross-validation is the honest tool.

Work the example by hand once: squaring turns residuals [1, 0, -2, 3] into [1, 0, 4, 9], so the single error of 3 supplies 9 of the 14 units of squared error, 64% of the total. That is the concrete meaning of 'MSE is dominated by large errors'.

RMSE = sqrt(3.5) = 1.87 is larger than MAE = 1.5, and the ratio 1.25 is a quick outlier gauge: a ratio near 1 means uniform errors, a ratio well above 1.5 suggests heavy tails worth inspecting.

SS_tot = 2.25 + 0.25 + 6.25 + 12.25 = 21 is the error of always predicting 4.5. The model removes a third of it, so R^2 = 0.33. With four points, adjusted R^2 for even one feature becomes 1 - 0.67 x 3/2 = 0.0, a reminder of how little tiny samples can support.

MAPE has three structural problems. Division by y makes it undefined at zero and enormous near it, which rules it out for intermittent demand, temperature in Celsius or any target that crosses zero. It is asymmetric: for a fixed actual, under-forecasting can cost at most 100% while over-forecasting is unbounded, so models selected by MAPE are biased low. And averaging per-row percentages weights a 1-unit item the same as a 10,000-unit item.

Alternatives: WAPE (sum of absolute errors divided by sum of actuals) is volume-weighted and stable; sMAPE divides by the average of |y| and |y_hat| but has its own asymmetry and still breaks when both are zero; MASE (mean absolute scaled error) divides MAE by the MAE of a naive seasonal forecast, so values below 1 beat the naive baseline. In retail and supply-chain work WAPE and MASE are the usual defaults.

A residual plot checks the assumptions behind your metric and your loss. Plot residuals against predictions rather than against true y: against y, even a perfect regression-to-the-mean pattern shows a misleading slope.

Patterns and remedies: a funnel (heteroscedasticity) suggests modeling log y, using a relative-error loss, or predicting variance explicitly; a curve means a missing nonlinearity or interaction, so add features or a more flexible model; clusters or stripes often mean a categorical variable the model ignores or a rounded target; a few points with huge residuals deserve inspection for label errors before you switch to a robust loss.

Complement the scatter with a histogram or Q-Q plot of residuals to judge whether tails are Gaussian, and with a calibration-style plot of mean y versus binned predictions to check for systematic bias across the prediction range.

Choosing a metric is choosing a cost function for errors, so start from the decision the predictions feed. If the cost of an error grows faster than linearly, as with capacity planning where a big shortfall causes outages, RMSE matches. If every unit of error costs the same, as with many pricing or time estimates, MAE is the honest summary. If stakeholders think in percentages and the target stays well away from zero, WAPE communicates best.

Always report a baseline: predicting the training mean (or, for time series, last value or same-day-last-week). A model with RMSE 12 means nothing until you know the baseline scores 13 or 40. Report several metrics when audiences differ, but optimize and select on one primary metric chosen in advance. For business decisions with asymmetric costs, consider a custom metric that literally computes expected cost.

On training data, R^2 cannot decrease when a feature is added to an OLS model, because the optimizer can always set the new coefficient to zero. That makes training R^2 useless for feature selection; noise features raise it.

Scale dependence bites in multi-target or multi-dataset reports: averaging RMSE across products with different sales volumes lets the largest products dominate. Normalize first (for example by the target's mean or standard deviation) or use a scaled metric such as MASE.

Other traps: computing metrics on a log scale and reporting them as if they were in original units; leaking future data into time-series validation; evaluating on a test set with a different target distribution than production. For the check question: MAE = (1 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 3, while RMSE = sqrt((1 + 1 + 1 + 81)/4) = sqrt(21) = 4.58. One large error moves RMSE far more.
ml-metrics-03.further: Learn proper scoring for full predictive distributions: CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) generalizes MAE to probabilistic forecasts, and interval coverage checks whether 90% prediction intervals really contain 90% of outcomes. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free intervals with coverage guarantees. For forecasting specifically, study MASE and the M-competition evaluation protocols, rolling-origin backtesting, and hierarchical reconciliation. Finally, read about heteroscedastic regression, where the model predicts both a mean and a variance, which turns residual-plot diagnosis into part of the model itself.

Ranking evaluation needs three ingredients: a query set that represents real traffic, relevance judgments for the returned items, and a cutoff k that matches what users actually see, such as 10 results on a page or 5 chunks in a RAG context window.

Judgments can be binary or graded (for example 0 irrelevant, 1 partial, 2 good, 3 perfect). Graded labels capture that a perfect answer at rank 1 beats a partial one, but they are more expensive and noisier, so measure inter-annotator agreement. Most offline benchmarks use pooling: only the top results from several systems get judged, and everything else is assumed irrelevant. That assumption is the source of several pitfalls later on.

Report metrics as an average over queries (macro average) so that each information need counts equally, and keep per-query scores for significance tests and error analysis.

Precision@k and recall@k trade off just like classification precision and recall, with k playing the role of the threshold: larger k raises recall and usually lowers precision. Recall@k needs the total number of relevant items per query, which is often unknown in web-scale search; it is natural in RAG and recommendation where a fixed gold set exists.

Hit rate@k (also called success@k or top-k accuracy) is the fraction of queries with at least one relevant item in the top k. It is the right metric when one good result is enough, such as question answering with a single gold passage. With exactly one relevant item per query, hit rate@k equals recall@k.

All three are set-based within the top k: swapping ranks 1 and k does not change them. That makes them stable and easy to explain, but blind to whether the best result is visible without scrolling.

Reciprocal rank is 1/r for the first relevant item at rank r, and 0 if none appears within the cutoff. MRR suits navigational or single-answer tasks: it cares only about the first hit, and moves quickly from rank 1 (1.0) to rank 2 (0.5) to rank 10 (0.1), so it is dominated by the top few positions.

Average precision rewards getting all relevant items early. For each relevant item at rank i, take precision@i, sum them, and divide by the total number of relevant items (not just those retrieved), so missing items count as zero. AP equals the area under the precision-recall curve for that query. MAP averages AP over queries.

Both are binary-relevance metrics. MAP was the standard in TREC-style document retrieval; MRR is common for question answering and code search. Neither handles graded relevance, which is where NDCG comes in.

DCG sums gains discounted by log2(i + 1), so rank 1 gets weight 1, rank 2 gets 0.63, rank 3 gets 0.50 and rank 10 gets 0.29. Two gain functions are common: rel_i itself, or 2^rel - 1, which strongly rewards highly relevant items (a grade 3 is worth 7, a grade 1 is worth 1). Always state which one you use, because scores are not comparable across conventions.

Normalization divides by IDCG, the DCG of the best possible ordering of the judged items for that query, so every query scores between 0 and 1 and averages are meaningful. A subtle choice: compute IDCG from all known relevant items, or only from those retrieved. The first is stricter and standard.

NDCG is the default for web search and recommendation ranking. Its logarithmic discount is a convention rather than a user model, so some teams prefer expected reciprocal rank (ERR) or rank-biased precision with an explicit patience parameter.

Trace each number. Relevant items sit at ranks 2, 3 and 5. Precision@3 = 2/3 and recall@3 = 2 of 3 relevant = 2/3. The first hit is at rank 2, so reciprocal rank = 0.5.

Average precision uses precision at each relevant rank: P@2 = 1/2, P@3 = 2/3, P@5 = 3/5. Their mean is 0.589. Had the same three items appeared at ranks 1 to 3, AP would be 1.0; the empty rank 1 costs a lot.

For NDCG with binary gains, DCG@5 = 1/log2(3) + 1/log2(4) + 1/log2(6) = 0.631 + 0.500 + 0.387 = 1.518. The ideal list puts all three relevant items first: 1 + 0.631 + 0.5 = 2.131. NDCG@5 = 0.712. Notice how the metrics disagree in magnitude: they answer different questions, so pick by user behavior, not by which number looks best.

Offline evaluation is cheap, reproducible and safe, so it is the filter for which candidates reach users. But labels go stale, pooled judgments miss what a new system finds, and offline metrics do not capture presentation, latency or diversity effects.

Online evaluation measures real behavior: click-through rate, time to first click, dwell time, reformulation rate, abandonment, downstream conversion. Clicks are position-biased (users click rank 1 partly because it is rank 1), so raw click logs make the incumbent ranking look good. Counterfactual methods such as inverse propensity weighting correct for this when learning from logs.

Interleaving is a powerful online method for ranking: merge results from systems A and B into one list per user and credit clicks to the source system. It typically needs one to two orders of magnitude less traffic than a classic A/B test to detect the same preference. Agreement between offline NDCG and online wins should be tracked over time.

RAG evaluation splits into retrieval and generation. For retrieval, build a set of questions with known supporting passages and measure recall@k at the k you actually feed the model; a passage that is not retrieved cannot be used. Then measure ordering with MRR or NDCG, because models attend unevenly over long contexts and relevant chunks buried in the middle are used less.

Context precision (what fraction of retrieved chunks are relevant) matters too: irrelevant chunks cost tokens and can distract or mislead the generator.

For generation, grade faithfulness (is every claim supported by the retrieved context?) separately from answer correctness. A correct answer from unsupported parametric memory is a faithfulness failure. LLM-as-a-judge graders are common for both, but validate them against human labels. Chunking, embedding model, hybrid lexical plus vector search and reranking are the usual levers on the retrieval side.

Incomplete judgments are the biggest offline trap. If a new retriever surfaces relevant documents nobody judged, pooled evaluation scores them as misses and penalizes innovation. Remedies: judge the new system's top results before comparing, use metrics robust to missing labels (such as bpref or condensed lists that drop unjudged items), or report the fraction of unjudged items in the top k.

Averaging hides tails: a system can raise mean NDCG while failing badly on rare but important query types. Slice by query category and frequency, and inspect the worst queries.

Cutoff effects: when a query has only two relevant items, precision@10 cannot exceed 0.2, so it mixes system quality with query difficulty. R-precision (precision at R, the number of relevant items) fixes that. Finally, k, gain function and averaging scheme must be reported, and significance should be tested per query with a paired test or bootstrap.
ml-metrics-04.further: Read about learning to rank (pointwise, pairwise and listwise methods such as LambdaMART) to see how these metrics become training objectives. Study counterfactual evaluation and unbiased learning to rank from click logs, interleaving experiments, and diversity-aware metrics such as alpha-NDCG for result sets that should cover several intents. For RAG specifically, look at reranking with cross-encoders, hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval, and evaluation frameworks that score context recall, context precision and faithfulness with LLM judges validated against human labels.

Formally, a binary classifier is calibrated if P(Y = 1 | score = p) = p for every p. For multiclass models there are several strengths: top-label (confidence) calibration only checks the predicted class's probability; classwise calibration checks each class's probability separately; full calibration requires the whole probability vector to be correct and is rarely testable.

Calibration matters whenever probabilities are used as probabilities: expected-cost decisions, risk scores in medicine and lending, ensembling or combining models, abstaining when uncertain, and setting thresholds that must transfer across populations. It matters much less if you only rank items or take an argmax.

Note that calibration alone is cheap: predicting the base rate for every example is perfectly calibrated but useless. A good model must be both calibrated and sharp, meaning it confidently separates cases. Proper scoring rules measure the two together.

A reliability diagram groups predictions into bins by confidence, then plots each bin's mean predicted confidence against its observed accuracy or positive rate. Equal-width bins (0.0-0.1, 0.1-0.2, ...) are common, but modern models put most predictions in the top bin, leaving others nearly empty and noisy. Equal-mass bins, each holding the same number of predictions, give more stable estimates.

Always show a histogram of bin counts beneath the diagram so readers know which points are reliable. Adding bootstrap error bars per bin helps distinguish real miscalibration from sampling noise.

Shape reading: points below the diagonal at high confidence are overconfidence, typical of large neural networks trained to near-zero training loss. A sigmoid-shaped curve, where predictions are pushed away from 0 and 1, was typical of boosted trees and SVMs in early studies and is what Platt scaling was designed to fix; naive Bayes shows the opposite, pushing predictions toward 0 and 1.

ECE is a weighted average of per-bin gaps, with weights equal to the share of predictions in each bin. Maximum calibration error (MCE) takes the worst bin instead, which matters for high-stakes settings.

ECE is a biased, binning-dependent estimator. With few samples per bin, random noise produces a positive gap even for a perfectly calibrated model, so ECE is biased upward on small test sets. Changing from 10 to 15 bins or from equal-width to equal-mass bins can reorder models. Report the bin count and scheme, and compare models with the same settings.

ECE is not a proper scoring rule: a model can lower ECE by becoming less informative, for example by predicting the base rate. That is why it should be reported alongside a proper score such as log loss or Brier. Variants include classwise ECE, adaptive ECE with equal-mass bins, and kernel or smoothed estimators that avoid hard bins.

Work through the gaps. Bin A holds 60 of 100 predictions with average confidence 0.90 but only 75% correct: a gap of 0.15, overconfident. Bin B holds 40 predictions at confidence 0.60 with 55% correct: a gap of 0.05, also overconfident. Weighting by share gives 0.6 x 0.15 + 0.4 x 0.05 = 0.09 + 0.02 = 0.11.

Interpretation: on average the model's stated confidence is 11 points away from its actual hit rate, and the error is concentrated in the high-confidence bin, which is exactly where users trust it most.

A quick sanity check on the overall level: mean confidence is 0.6 x 0.90 + 0.4 x 0.60 = 0.78, while accuracy is 0.6 x 0.75 + 0.4 x 0.55 = 0.67. A gap of 0.11 between average confidence and accuracy suggests a single temperature T > 1 would fix most of it.

Brier score and log loss are strictly proper scoring rules: in expectation they are minimized only by reporting the true probability, so they cannot be gamed by hedging. Both reward calibration and sharpness together.

The Brier score decomposes (Murphy decomposition) into reliability (calibration error) minus resolution (how much predictions vary with outcomes) plus uncertainty (the base-rate variance). Its range is 0 to 1 for binary outcomes; a constant 0.5 forecast scores 0.25 regardless of the data, and the base-rate forecast scores p(1 - p).

Log loss is the negative log-likelihood of the labels. It is unbounded: a confident miss at p = 0.99 costs -ln(0.01) = 4.6 nats, while a correct 0.99 costs 0.01. This makes it sensitive to a handful of catastrophic predictions and to label noise. Brier is more forgiving. Both should be compared with the base-rate forecast, for example via a Brier skill score.

All post-hoc methods learn a mapping from the model's score to a probability using data the model was not trained on: a validation split, or out-of-fold predictions from cross-validation. Fitting on training data learns nothing, because training predictions are overconfident in a different way.

Platt scaling fits sigmoid(a x s + b) to the scores s with logistic regression; it is low-variance and works well when miscalibration is S-shaped. Isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function; it can fix any monotone distortion but overfits small calibration sets and creates ties. Temperature scaling, the standard for neural networks, divides all logits by a single T fitted by minimizing validation NLL; it preserves the argmax and accuracy and works surprisingly well. Extensions include vector and matrix scaling, beta calibration, and histogram binning. In scikit-learn, CalibratedClassifierCV implements Platt (method sigmoid) and isotonic.

Discrimination measures whether a model separates classes, regardless of the actual numbers: AUROC is the probability a random positive scores above a random negative. Calibration measures whether the numbers mean what they say. The two are logically independent: any strictly increasing transform of the scores leaves AUROC unchanged but can wreck or repair calibration.

That is why recalibration is a free lunch for ranking. Platt scaling on a binary score preserves order exactly. Temperature scaling preserves each example's argmax, but in multiclass settings it can change the ordering of one class's probabilities across examples, so one-vs-rest AUROC can shift slightly. Isotonic regression can create ties that change AUROC a little.

In practice report both: AUROC or AUPRC for ranking and a proper score plus ECE or a reliability diagram for probabilities. Interviewers like asking which one should drive model selection; the answer depends on whether downstream decisions use ranks or probabilities.

Calibration is a property of a model on a distribution, not of the model alone. Under covariate shift or a change in class prevalence, a well-calibrated model drifts: if fraud doubles in production, every probability is too low. Prior-shift correction (reweighting by the ratio of new to old base rates) helps for label shift; otherwise recalibrate on fresh labeled data.

Large modern networks tend to be overconfident, as shown by Guo et al. (2017). For LLMs, pretrained models are often fairly well calibrated on multiple-choice token probabilities, while RLHF and other post-training commonly make them overconfident. Verbalized confidence ('I am 90% sure') is a different signal and needs its own evaluation.

Also check calibration per class and per subgroup, since an average can hide groups that are systematically over- or under-estimated, which is both an accuracy and a fairness problem. Finally, report how many samples support each bin.
ml-metrics-05.further: Explore proper scoring rule theory (Gneiting and Raftery), the Murphy decomposition of the Brier score, and decision curves that convert calibrated probabilities into expected net benefit. For deep learning, read about calibration under distribution shift, deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout as uncertainty estimates, and conformal prediction for guaranteed coverage sets. For LLMs, look into calibration of token probabilities versus verbalized confidence, selective prediction with abstention, and how post-training changes calibration.

A hypothesis test is a decision procedure with known error rates. You choose a test statistic (difference in means, difference in proportions, a z or t score), derive its distribution under H0, and reject H0 when the observed statistic falls in a region that has probability alpha under H0.

Two error types: Type I (false positive, rejecting a true H0) happens at rate alpha by construction; Type II (false negative, missing a real effect) happens at rate beta, and power = 1 - beta. Two-sided tests look for differences in either direction and are the default; one-sided tests are only legitimate if you committed in advance to ignore effects in the other direction.

The unit of randomization matters: if you randomize users but analyze page views, observations are correlated and naive standard errors are too small. Use the randomization unit, or cluster-robust or delta-method variance estimates.

The p-value is computed assuming H0 is true, so it cannot be the probability that H0 is true. Converting to that probability requires a prior, which is what Bayesian analysis does explicitly. With a low prior chance of a real effect, as in many product experiments where most ideas fail, a large share of p < 0.05 results can be false positives.

A tiny p does not mean a big effect: with millions of users, a 0.01% lift can be highly significant and commercially meaningless. Conversely, p = 0.2 in an underpowered test is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence; the confidence interval will show that large effects remain plausible.

The 0.05 threshold is a convention. The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement warns against treating it as a bright line. Report exact p-values, effect sizes and intervals, and avoid language like 'trending toward significance'.

A 95% confidence interval is produced by a procedure that captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated experiments. Strictly, it is not a 95% probability statement about this particular interval; that Bayesian interpretation needs a prior, though with weak priors and large samples the numbers are close.

For a difference in proportions, a Wald interval is diff +/- 1.96 x sqrt(pA(1 - pA)/nA + pB(1 - pB)/nB). It behaves poorly for rates near 0 or 1 or tiny samples; Wilson or Newcombe intervals are better there. For relative lift (B/A - 1), use the delta method or a log-ratio interval.

A CI and a two-sided test built from the same standard error agree: the 95% CI excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05. CIs are more informative because they show which effect sizes remain plausible, and you can compare the interval with a practical significance threshold, for example 'any lift above 0.5 points is worth shipping'.

Power depends on four quantities: significance level alpha, sample size n, the variance of the metric, and the true effect size. Fixing three determines the fourth. The usual workflow fixes alpha = 0.05, power = 80% and a minimum detectable effect the business cares about, then solves for n.

The rule of thumb n per arm = 16 x variance / delta^2 comes from (z_0.975 + z_0.80)^2 x 2 = (1.96 + 0.84)^2 x 2 = 15.7. For a conversion rate p, variance is p(1 - p). Halving the MDE quadruples the required sample, which is why detecting small lifts takes so long.

Variance reduction buys power without more users: CUPED regresses out pre-experiment behavior and often cuts variance by 20-50%; stratification and trimming heavy-tailed metrics help too. Underpowered tests are dangerous beyond missing effects: the significant results they do produce systematically overestimate the effect size, the so-called winner's curse.

Planning: baseline 10%, so variance p(1 - p) = 0.09, and an MDE of 1 percentage point gives n = 16 x 0.09 / 0.0001 = 14,400 users per arm, 28,800 total.

Analysis: pA = 0.100 and pB = 0.111. The difference is 0.0111. Standard error = sqrt(0.1 x 0.9 / 14,400 + 0.111 x 0.889 / 14,400) = 0.00362. z = 0.0111 / 0.00362 = 3.07, two-sided p = 0.002. The 95% CI is 0.0111 +/- 1.96 x 0.00362 = [0.40, 1.82] percentage points, a relative lift between roughly 4% and 18%.

Decision: the interval excludes 0 and its center exceeds the planned MDE, so shipping is justified. Before shipping, check a sample ratio mismatch (were the arms really 50/50?), guardrail metrics such as latency and refunds, and whether the effect holds across major segments.

With m independent tests at alpha = 0.05 and no true effects, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^m: 40% for m = 10 and 64% for m = 20. Testing many metrics, segments or variants without correction almost guarantees a spurious win.

Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at alpha / m, controlling the family-wise error rate (FWER, the chance of any false positive). It is valid under any dependence but conservative. Holm's step-down procedure controls FWER with more power and should usually replace plain Bonferroni.

Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate: sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k) <= (k/m) x q, and reject the first k. It suits exploratory screens with many metrics. The cleanest defense is design: pre-register one primary metric and decision rule, label secondary metrics as exploratory, and treat segment findings as hypotheses for a follow-up test.

Comparing models on a shared test set should be paired, because both models see the same examples and their errors are correlated. Unpaired tests waste that structure and lose power.

For accuracy, McNemar's test uses only the discordant examples (A right and B wrong, versus the reverse). For any metric, the paired bootstrap resamples examples with replacement, computes the metric difference for both models on each resample, and reads a percentile interval from typically 1,000 to 10,000 resamples. The percentile interval is simple; BCa intervals correct for bias and skew. The bootstrap assumes examples are independent; for grouped data (several questions per document, several turns per conversation) resample whole groups.

Training randomness is a second source of variance: different seeds can move scores by more than the claimed improvement. Train several seeds per method and report mean and spread. Same data splits, preprocessing and tuning budget are part of fairness too.

A fixed-sample test controls alpha only if you analyze once at the planned n. Each extra look gives noise another chance to cross the threshold; with continuous monitoring the false-positive rate approaches 100% over a long enough horizon. Armitage and colleagues showed about 19% with 10 equally spaced looks.

Valid ways to monitor: group sequential designs with alpha spending functions (O'Brien-Fleming spends very little alpha early), always-valid inference such as mixture sequential probability ratio tests, and Bayesian monitoring with pre-specified decision rules. Many experimentation platforms implement one of these.

Other practical traps: novelty and primacy effects make early results unrepresentative, so run full weekly cycles; sample ratio mismatch (for example 50.8% vs 49.2% on large traffic) indicates a broken assignment or logging bug and invalidates results; and interference between users, as in marketplaces or social networks, breaks the independence assumption and calls for cluster or switchback designs.
ml-metrics-06.further: Next steps: sequential testing and always-valid p-values, CUPED and other variance-reduction methods, Bayesian A/B testing with decision-theoretic stopping, and multi-armed bandits for when exploration cost matters more than inference. Study the delta method for ratio metrics, heterogeneous treatment effects for segment analysis, and network or marketplace experiment designs. For ML research, read about statistical rigor in benchmark comparisons: seeds, paired bootstraps, and reporting confidence intervals on leaderboards.

A loss must be cheap to evaluate per example and provide gradients that point toward better models. That excludes many business metrics: accuracy, MAPE with zero targets, median absolute error and rank-based scores are flat or non-differentiable, so we train on a smooth surrogate and report the metric.

The loss also encodes a statistical assumption. Minimizing expected loss gives a specific functional of the conditional distribution of y given x: the mean for squared loss, the median for absolute loss, a quantile for pinball loss. Choosing a loss therefore chooses what your model's output means.

Total training objective = data loss + regularization (weight decay, dropout effects) and sometimes auxiliary terms. Early stopping and model selection should use the metric you care about on validation data, even if training used a different loss. When loss and metric disagree badly, consider a loss closer to the metric, or post-hoc adjustment such as shifting predictions.

If y = f(x) + noise with Gaussian noise of fixed variance sigma^2, the negative log-likelihood of a dataset is sum (y - f(x))^2 / (2 sigma^2) plus a constant. Minimizing it is exactly least squares, which is why MSE is the default for regression and why linear regression with MSE has a closed-form solution.

The gradient with respect to the prediction is -2e, so an error of 10 pushes 10 times harder than an error of 1. That gives fast convergence when errors are small and well-behaved, but lets a few outliers or mislabeled points dominate training.

If noise variance differs across examples (heteroscedasticity), plain MSE is no longer the maximum-likelihood estimator. A Gaussian NLL loss that predicts both mean and variance, such as torch.nn.GaussianNLLLoss, learns where the model is uncertain and down-weights noisy regions automatically.

Absolute loss corresponds to Laplace-distributed noise, whose heavier tails make large deviations more plausible, so the fit is less disturbed by them. The constant minimizing sum |y - c| is any median of the data, which is why MAE regression is also called least absolute deviations or median regression.

The gradient is sign(e): every example pushes with the same force regardless of error size. This makes MAE robust, but optimization is harder. Near the optimum the gradient does not shrink, so gradient descent oscillates unless the learning rate decays; the kink at zero has no derivative (frameworks use a subgradient of 0). Linear MAE regression is solved exactly as a linear program.

Robustness has limits: MAE handles outliers in y but not high-leverage outliers in x. And if the conditional distribution is skewed, median and mean differ, so an MAE model will appear biased when evaluated by MSE.

Huber loss is the classic robust M-estimator: quadratic within delta, so small errors get MSE's smooth, shrinking gradients, and linear beyond delta, so each outlier's gradient is capped at magnitude delta. The two pieces join with matching value and slope at |e| = delta, giving a continuous first derivative.

Choosing delta: a common statistical default is about 1.345 times the noise standard deviation, which keeps 95% efficiency under Gaussian noise while resisting outliers. In deep learning, delta = 1 on standardized targets is typical. As delta grows the loss approaches 0.5 x MSE; as it shrinks it approaches delta x MAE.

Smooth L1 loss, used in object-detection box regression, is Huber divided by delta (with parameter beta). Pseudo-Huber, delta^2 (sqrt(1 + (e/delta)^2) - 1), is smooth everywhere, which helps second-order optimizers. Log-cosh loss behaves similarly. For gross outliers, redescending losses such as Tukey's biweight ignore extreme points entirely but are non-convex.

Pinball loss for quantile q weights positive residuals (under-prediction) by q and negative ones by 1 - q. The minimizer of expected pinball loss is the q-th conditional quantile, so training with q = 0.9 produces predictions that true values fall below 90% of the time, if the model is well specified.

Prediction intervals come from training several quantiles, either in separate models or as multiple output heads sharing a backbone. Independent heads can cross (the 0.9 prediction below the 0.5 prediction); enforce monotonicity by predicting positive increments, or sort outputs. Check empirical coverage on held-out data: the fraction of targets inside the 0.1-0.9 band should be near 80%.

Gradient boosting libraries support quantile objectives natively (LightGBM objective='quantile' with alpha). Conformalized quantile regression wraps these predictions with a calibration step to guarantee coverage. Pinball loss averaged across many quantiles approximates CRPS, the standard proper score for probabilistic forecasts.

The constant c minimizing squared loss is the mean: setting the derivative sum -2(y_i - c) to zero gives c = mean(y) = 110/5 = 22, a value no data point is near. Absolute loss gives the median, 3, because moving c away from the middle point increases distances to more points than it decreases.

For Huber with delta = 1, the optimality condition is that clipped residuals sum to zero. At c = 3 the residuals are -2, -1, 0, 1, 97, clipped to -1, -1, 0, 1, 1, which sum to 0, so c = 3. The outlier contributes a gradient of only +1 instead of +97. With delta = 3 the solution moves to 3.25: a larger delta lets the outlier pull a bit more.

The lesson generalizes: one corrupted label in a batch can dominate the MSE gradient for that step, which is why noisy-label datasets often train better with Huber or MAE.

Compare values at e = 10: squared 100, Huber with delta 1 gives 9.5, absolute 10. At e = 0.1, squared gives 0.01 and absolute 0.1, so MSE essentially ignores tiny errors and MAE keeps pushing on them. That is the outlier behavior plot in numbers: quadratic losses magnify large errors, linear ones treat all errors proportionally.

Decision guide. Roughly Gaussian noise and a need for the mean, for example when predictions are summed into totals, means MSE: means aggregate correctly, medians do not. Heavy-tailed noise, corrupted labels or a need for a typical value means Huber, or MAE if you can tolerate slower optimization. Asymmetric costs, service-level targets, or uncertainty bands mean quantile loss. Count data suggests Poisson loss; strictly positive skewed data suggests Gamma or Tweedie losses, which are common in insurance and demand forecasting.

Target scale interacts with loss and optimizer. MSE on targets in the millions produces enormous gradients that destabilize training and swamp regularization; standardize targets (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) and invert the transform at prediction time. Remember that Huber's delta and quantile intervals then live in standardized units.

Log transforms are tempting for skewed targets but change the estimand. Minimizing MSE on log y estimates E[log y | x]; exponentiating gives the geometric mean, which equals the median for lognormal data and is below the mean. If you need the mean (for revenue totals), apply a correction such as multiplying by exp(sigma^2 / 2) or use a Gamma or Tweedie loss on the raw scale.

Other traps: mixing loss reductions (sum vs mean) changes the effective learning rate with batch size, and per-example weights quietly change what the minimizer means.
ml-losses-01.further: Go deeper with generalized linear models and their losses (Poisson, Gamma, Tweedie deviance), heteroscedastic regression that predicts a mean and variance, and mixture density networks for multimodal targets. Study robust statistics (M-estimators, breakdown point, Tukey's biweight), quantile regression forests and conformalized quantile regression for calibrated intervals, and CRPS as a training loss for probabilistic forecasting. The link between loss choice and Bayes-optimal predictions is the key unifying idea.

panels:
Cross-entropy between the one-hot label and the predicted distribution reduces to -log p_true, which is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model. Minimizing it makes predicted probabilities match empirical class frequencies, which is why cross-entropy-trained models can be calibrated in principle.

The gradient with respect to the logits is p - y: the predicted probability vector minus the one-hot target. It is bounded in [-1, 1] per component, never vanishes while the model is wrong, and shrinks as the model becomes right. That clean form comes from pairing softmax with log loss; pairing softmax with MSE gives gradients that vanish when the model is confidently wrong.

Accuracy is piecewise constant in the parameters, with zero gradient almost everywhere. Cross-entropy is a convex surrogate in the logits, an upper bound on 0-1 loss up to scaling, and statistically consistent: its minimizer also minimizes classification error.

Softmax of [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]: exponentials are 7.39, 2.72 and 1.11, summing to 11.21, so p = [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]. Softmax depends only on differences between logits, so adding a constant to every logit changes nothing; implementations subtract the max logit before exponentiating to avoid overflow.

Loss for true class 0: -ln 0.659 = 0.417. Had the label been class 2, the loss would be 2.317, more than five times larger, reflecting that the model gave it only 10%.

Gradient for true class 0: p - y = [0.659 - 1, 0.242, 0.099] = [-0.341, 0.242, 0.099]. A gradient-descent step subtracts this, raising logit 0 and lowering the others in proportion to how much probability they stole. The components sum to zero, which is a handy correctness check when implementing softmax cross-entropy by hand.

The naive computation log(sigmoid(z)) fails in floating point. For z = -800, sigmoid returns exactly 0 in float32 and log gives -inf, so the loss becomes inf and gradients NaN. For large positive z, 1 - sigmoid(z) rounds to 0 with the same problem on negative labels.

The stable formulation rewrites the loss directly in terms of z: max(z, 0) - z*y + log(1 + exp(-|z|)). The exponent is never positive, so nothing overflows, and log1p keeps precision when exp(-|z|) is tiny. Multiclass cross-entropy uses the same log-sum-exp trick.

Practical rules: output raw logits from the model; use BCEWithLogitsLoss or binary_cross_entropy_with_logits in PyTorch (from_logits=True in Keras); only apply sigmoid at inference time. The pos_weight argument rescales positive examples, useful for imbalance. Mixed-precision training makes these issues more frequent, which is why fused loss kernels compute in float32 internally.

Hinge loss penalizes examples that are misclassified or classified correctly but with margin below 1. Once y f(x) >= 1 the loss and gradient are exactly zero, so only examples near or across the boundary, the support vectors, influence the solution. Combined with L2 regularization, this yields the maximum-margin classifier of a support vector machine.

Compared with logistic loss, hinge is not differentiable at margin 1 (subgradients handle that) and never produces probabilities: an SVM score is a distance-like margin, which needs Platt scaling to become a probability. Logistic loss keeps pushing confident correct examples, slowly, which tends to give better probability estimates.

Variants: squared hinge is smooth and penalizes violations quadratically; multiclass hinge (Crammer-Singer) requires the true class score to beat every other class by a margin; and margin-based ideas reappear in contrastive and triplet losses for embeddings.

Focal loss, introduced for RetinaNet, multiplies cross-entropy by (1 - p_t)^gamma. With gamma = 0 it is ordinary cross-entropy. With gamma = 2, an example at p_t = 0.9 contributes 0.01 times its cross-entropy, and at p_t = 0.99 only 0.0001 times, while hard examples at p_t = 0.1 keep 81% of their loss.

The original paper also uses an alpha weight per class (alpha = 0.25 for positives, interacting with gamma) and initializes the final bias so the model starts predicting a low foreground probability, around 0.01, which stabilizes early training.

Trade-offs: focal loss changes the minimizer, so its outputs are systematically underconfident on easy examples and not calibrated; recalibrate if you need probabilities. It shines when a flood of easy negatives drowns the gradient, such as dense detection or segmentation. For moderately imbalanced tabular data, class weights plus threshold tuning are usually simpler and just as good.

Label smoothing replaces the one-hot target with (1 - eps) on the true class plus eps/K spread over all K classes. With hard targets, cross-entropy is minimized only as the logit gap goes to infinity, so the model keeps growing logits; smoothing gives a finite optimum and acts as a regularizer. It was popularized by Inception-v3 and the original Transformer (eps = 0.1).

Effects: often better generalization and calibration for large classifiers, tighter clusters in the penultimate layer, but it erases information about which wrong classes are similar, which can hurt knowledge distillation from a smoothed teacher.

Class weights multiply each example's loss by a weight for its class, commonly inverse frequency or the smoother effective number of samples. They shift the decision boundary toward the minority class, equivalent in expectation to resampling. They also shift predicted probabilities away from true frequencies, so recalibrate or adjust the threshold before reading outputs as probabilities.

The double-softmax bug is common: nn.CrossEntropyLoss already applies log-softmax, so feeding it softmax outputs squashes probabilities into a narrow range, weakens gradients and slows learning without obvious errors. Similarly, nn.NLLLoss expects log-probabilities, not probabilities.

Numerical failures: computing log of probabilities that underflowed to 0 gives -inf and NaN gradients. Use fused losses on logits, or clamp probabilities if you must work in probability space. Label errors are another hazard: cross-entropy punishes confident disagreement with a wrong label very hard, so noisy datasets benefit from label smoothing or robust losses such as generalized cross-entropy.

Reweighting and focal terms change the optimum, so the outputs are no longer estimates of the true class probabilities. If downstream logic uses probabilities, for example expected cost, ranking across classes or abstention, recalibrate on unweighted validation data. Also check the reduction mode, ignore_index for padding tokens, and the expected label format (indices vs one-hot or soft targets).

Cross-entropy is measured in nats when using natural logs. A uniform guess between two classes costs ln 2 = 0.693 nats, the coin-flip baseline. A confident miss at p_true = 0.01 costs ln 100 = 4.605 nats, about 6.6 times the coin flip, so one such mistake outweighs several honest guesses in the average.

Useful baselines to remember: for K balanced classes, a uniform predictor scores ln K (2.30 for 10 classes, 10.8 for a 50,000-token vocabulary). A model whose validation loss sits near ln K has learned nothing; loss well above ln K means it is confidently wrong, often a sign of label misalignment or a preprocessing bug.

This asymmetry is why log loss rewards hedging when uncertain and why a single mislabeled example with a confident prediction can dominate a small evaluation set. It is also why calibration and log loss are closely linked.
ml-losses-02.further: Next topics: proper scoring rules and why cross-entropy yields calibrated probabilities in the limit, robust losses for noisy labels (generalized cross-entropy, symmetric cross-entropy, co-teaching), logit adjustment and balanced softmax for long-tailed data, and knowledge distillation with soft targets and temperature. For large output spaces, study sampled softmax, hierarchical softmax and the memory-efficient fused cross-entropy kernels used in LLM training. Poly loss and asymmetric loss are useful focal-style variants for detection and multi-label tasks.

panels:
Contrastive learning turns supervision into comparisons. Positives can come from labels (same identity, same class), from data augmentation (two crops of the same image in SimCLR), from natural pairings (an image and its caption, a query and the clicked document), or from adjacency (neighboring sentences or video frames).

Embeddings are usually L2-normalized so that dot product equals cosine similarity and all points lie on a hypersphere. Normalization prevents the trivial solution of making vectors larger to increase similarity and makes temperature a meaningful scale.

Two properties describe a good embedding space: alignment (positives are close) and uniformity (embeddings spread evenly over the sphere, preserving information). Wang and Isola showed that the contrastive loss optimizes both. The learned encoder is then used for retrieval, clustering, zero-shot classification or as a pretrained backbone for downstream tasks.

The pairwise contrastive loss of Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun (2006) treats each pair independently. Similar pairs pay their squared distance, so they are pulled together. Dissimilar pairs pay only if they are closer than margin m, so they are pushed apart until they reach the margin and then contribute nothing. Without the margin, the loss would push negatives infinitely apart and dominate training.

Because each pair is scored in isolation, the loss imposes an absolute notion of distance: all similar pairs should be near 0 and all dissimilar ones beyond m, regardless of context. That is harder to satisfy than relative constraints when classes vary in spread.

Practical issues: the ratio of positive to negative pairs must be balanced, margins depend on embedding scale (normalize first), and most random negative pairs already exceed the margin, giving zero gradient. This motivated triplet losses and then multi-negative losses like InfoNCE.

The triplet loss (popularized by FaceNet) asks only for a relative ordering: the anchor must be closer to the positive than to the negative by at least margin m. In the example, d(a,p) = 0.4 and d(a,n) = 0.6, so the negative is closer than required: 0.4 - 0.6 + 0.5 = 0.3 > 0, and the gradient pulls p in and pushes n out.

The number of possible triplets grows cubically with dataset size and most are easy (zero loss), so triplet mining dominates practical success. FaceNet used semi-hard negatives within large batches. Batch-hard mining picks, for each anchor, the farthest positive and the closest negative in the batch.

Margins are typically 0.2 to 1.0 on normalized embeddings. Squared versus plain Euclidean distance changes the gradient profile. Soft-margin variants replace max(0, x) with log(1 + exp(x)) to avoid hand-tuning m and keep a small gradient on satisfied triplets.

InfoNCE frames contrastive learning as classification: identify the positive among N candidates. The loss is cross-entropy over similarity scores divided by temperature tau. Minimizing it maximizes a lower bound on the mutual information between the two views, a bound that tightens as N grows (it cannot exceed log N).

NT-Xent (normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy), used in SimCLR, is InfoNCE with cosine similarity, where each of 2N augmented views treats its partner as the positive and the other 2N - 2 views as negatives.

Temperature controls the shape of the distribution over negatives. The gradient on each negative is proportional to its softmax weight, so a small tau concentrates gradient on the hardest negatives, while a large tau treats negatives more uniformly. Typical values are 0.05 to 0.2; CLIP learns tau as a parameter, initialized at 0.07 and clipped to keep the logit scale at most 100.

CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder jointly on image-caption pairs (400 million in the original work). For a batch of N pairs it computes an N x N matrix of cosine similarities scaled by a learned temperature. Row i should put its maximum at column i (image i matches caption i), and column i should do the same for text-to-image retrieval. The loss averages the two cross-entropies, making it symmetric.

The batch size is critical: OpenAI used 32,768, giving each example 32,767 negatives. Large batches require distributed training with gathered embeddings across devices. SigLIP replaces softmax with an independent sigmoid loss per pair, which removes the global normalization and scales well to smaller or very large batches.

After training, zero-shot classification embeds prompts like 'a photo of a {label}' and picks the closest text embedding. The same recipe trains text embedding models for retrieval, with query-passage pairs instead of image-caption pairs.

As training progresses, random negatives become trivially separable, their softmax weights or triplet losses shrink to zero, and learning stalls. Hard negatives keep the task informative: in retrieval, BM25 or a previous model's top results that are not labeled relevant; in face recognition, other identities that look similar.

Semi-hard negatives are farther than the positive but still within the margin. They give useful gradient without the instability of the hardest negatives, which early in training can drive embeddings toward collapse.

The danger with very hard negatives is false negatives: in web-scale data, the closest non-labeled passage is often actually relevant, just unannotated, and training to push it away teaches the wrong thing. Mitigations include filtering negatives with a cross-encoder, skipping the top few candidates, or debiased contrastive losses that correct for the expected rate of false negatives. Refreshing mined negatives with the current model (as in ANCE) keeps them hard as the model improves.

Pairwise ranking losses only constrain relative scores. BPR (Rendle et al., 2009) was designed for implicit feedback: for a user, sample an interacted item i and a non-interacted item j, and maximize log sigmoid(s_i - s_j). It is the maximum a posteriori estimate under a model where the user prefers i over j, and it directly optimizes a smooth version of AUC per user.

RankNet (Burges et al., 2005) models P(i ranked above j) = sigmoid(s_i - s_j) and minimizes cross-entropy against target preferences, which can be soft when judgments are graded. LambdaRank and LambdaMART reweight each pair's gradient by the change in NDCG from swapping the two items, so pairs near the top of the list matter more; LambdaMART remains a strong baseline in learning to rank.

Listwise losses such as ListNet and softmax cross-entropy over the whole candidate list are closely related to InfoNCE and often outperform pairwise ones.

InfoNCE quality depends on the number and difficulty of negatives. Small batches can be compensated with a memory bank or momentum queue (MoCo keeps a queue of 65,536 keys encoded by a slowly updated momentum encoder), or by mining hard negatives explicitly.

False negatives inside a batch arise from duplicates, near-duplicates or semantically identical captions ('a dog on grass' appearing twice). Deduplicate data, or mask known duplicates out of the denominator.

Temperature that is too low produces sharp, high-variance gradients and can destabilize training; too high blurs the distinction between hard and easy negatives and yields less discriminative embeddings. Monitor alignment and uniformity, or embedding-variance statistics, to detect collapse early.

Non-contrastive methods such as BYOL, SimSiam and VICReg avoid negatives entirely, preventing collapse with predictor networks, stop-gradients or variance and covariance regularizers. They are useful when negatives are expensive or noisy.
ml-losses-03.further: Study the mutual-information view of InfoNCE and its log N limit, supervised contrastive learning (SupCon), and debiased and hard-negative-aware objectives. For retrieval, read about dense passage retrieval, ANCE, in-batch versus cross-batch negatives, and distilling cross-encoder rerankers into bi-encoders. Explore non-contrastive self-supervised learning (BYOL, VICReg, DINO), SigLIP's sigmoid loss, Matryoshka embeddings, and listwise learning-to-rank objectives such as LambdaMART and softmax ranking losses.

panels:
Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameters that maximize p_theta(data). Because data points are assumed independent, the likelihood is a product, and taking logs turns it into a sum, which is numerically stable and decomposes into per-example losses suitable for stochastic gradient descent.

Minimizing average NLL is equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy between the empirical data distribution and the model, and therefore to minimizing KL(data || model), since the data entropy is a constant. This forward-KL view explains why maximum likelihood is mass-covering: the model is heavily penalized for assigning near-zero probability to any observed example.

Many familiar losses are NLLs under some noise model: MSE for Gaussian, MAE for Laplace, cross-entropy for categorical, Poisson loss for counts. Adding a prior on parameters gives maximum a posteriori estimation, where a Gaussian prior is exactly L2 weight decay. MLE is consistent and efficient under correct specification, but overfits with flexible models.

An autoregressive model factorizes p(x) = product over t of p(x_t | x_<t), so the sequence NLL is the sum of per-token cross-entropies. Training uses teacher forcing: every position predicts the next true token in parallel, with a causal mask preventing the model from seeing the future. Loss is usually averaged over non-padding tokens, and in supervised fine-tuning often only over response tokens.

Perplexity exp(mean NLL) is the effective number of equally likely choices per token. A loss of 2.0 nats gives perplexity 7.4: the model is, on average, as uncertain as picking among 7.4 tokens. Losses are often quoted in bits (divide nats by ln 2) or bits per byte.

Next-token loss is what scaling laws predict: it falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute. But small differences in loss can hide large differences in downstream capabilities, and loss on a benchmark can be distorted by contamination.

KL(P || Q) is the expected extra code length, in nats or bits, from encoding samples of P with a code optimized for Q. It is non-negative (Gibbs' inequality) and zero only when the distributions match. It is not a distance: it is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality. Cross-entropy H(P, Q) = H(P) + KL(P || Q).

In the example, KL(P || Q) = 0.5 ln(0.5/0.9) + 0.5 ln(0.5/0.1) = 0.51 nats and KL(Q || P) = 0.9 ln 1.8 + 0.1 ln 0.2 = 0.37 nats.

Forward KL(P || Q) is infinite if Q assigns zero probability where P has mass, so the fitted Q spreads to cover all modes (mean-seeking). Reverse KL(Q || P) is infinite if Q puts mass where P has none, so Q hugs one mode (mode-seeking). Maximum likelihood minimizes forward KL; variational inference minimizes reverse KL; the KL penalty in RLHF is a reverse KL from the policy to the reference model.

For latent-variable models p(x) = integral p(x|z) p(z) dz, the likelihood is intractable. Introducing an approximate posterior q(z|x) from an encoder and applying Jensen's inequality gives log p(x) >= ELBO. The gap equals KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)), so maximizing the ELBO both improves the likelihood bound and makes q a better posterior.

The reconstruction term E_q[log p(x|z)] is estimated with one sampled z per example. Gradients flow through the sampling by the reparameterization trick: z = mu + sigma * eps with eps ~ N(0, I). The KL term between two Gaussians has a closed form: 0.5 sum (mu^2 + sigma^2 - log sigma^2 - 1).

The choice of decoder likelihood defines the reconstruction loss: Gaussian gives MSE (with a variance that sets the balance against KL), Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy. beta-VAE scales the KL term to trade reconstruction quality for more disentangled, compressed latents.

The minimax objective was introduced by Goodfellow et al. (2014). For a fixed generator, the optimal discriminator is D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_G(x)); substituting it shows the generator minimizes 2 x JS(p_data || p_G) - log 4, where JS is the Jensen-Shannon divergence. So GANs do minimize a divergence, just implicitly, and never evaluate a likelihood.

Early in training the discriminator easily rejects fakes, D(G(z)) is near 0, and log(1 - D(G(z))) saturates with vanishing gradients. The non-saturating trick has G maximize log D(G(z)) instead, which has the same fixed point but strong gradients when G is poor.

Alternatives fix other instabilities: Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty uses an earth mover's distance critic; hinge-loss GANs and spectral normalization (as in BigGAN and StyleGAN) improve stability. GANs produce sharp samples quickly but are hard to train and evaluate; metrics such as FID compare feature statistics instead of likelihood.

Denoising diffusion models (DDPM, Ho et al. 2020) define a forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise. Because the composition of Gaussian steps is Gaussian, any noise level can be sampled directly: x_t = sqrt(a_bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - a_bar_t) eps, where a_bar_t is the cumulative product of the per-step signal retention and decreases from about 1 to about 0.

The network eps_theta(x_t, t) predicts the added noise. The full objective is an ELBO with a sum of KL terms per step; with fixed variances each term is a weighted MSE on the noise, and dropping the weights gives the simple loss that produces better samples. Equivalently, the model estimates the score, the gradient of log density, scaled by noise level.

Variants predict x_0 or the velocity v = sqrt(a_bar) eps - sqrt(1 - a_bar) x_0, and use different noise schedules and loss weightings. Flow matching trains a velocity field with a closely related regression loss and powers many current image and video models.

The families differ in what they can compute. Autoregressive models give exact log-likelihoods, which makes evaluation and comparison straightforward, but sampling is sequential. Normalizing flows also give exact likelihoods through invertible transforms with tractable Jacobians.

VAEs optimize a bound, so their reported NLL is an upper bound, tightened with importance-weighted estimates. Samples can be blurry when the decoder is a simple Gaussian, because MSE averages over plausible outputs.

GANs give no likelihood and are judged by sample-based metrics (FID, precision and recall of generated features). Training is a two-player game whose equilibrium may never be reached, causing oscillation and mode collapse.

Diffusion models optimize a reweighted bound; their likelihood can be estimated with an ODE formulation, and they sample with many network evaluations, reduced by distillation and better solvers. Modern systems mix ideas: latent diffusion with a VAE encoder, adversarial losses for distillation, and autoregressive models over discrete image tokens.

Perplexity is per token, so tokenizers with longer tokens have fewer, harder predictions and higher perplexity for the same total information. Compare models with different tokenizers using bits per byte or per character: total NLL in bits divided by the number of UTF-8 bytes.

Posterior collapse happens when a powerful decoder, such as an autoregressive one, models the data alone, so the optimal q(z|x) equals the prior and the KL term goes to zero. Fixes include KL annealing (warming up the KL weight), free bits that guarantee a minimum KL per dimension, and weaker or dropout-limited decoders.

Mode collapse in GANs means the generator covers only a few modes that fool the current discriminator. Diagnose with diversity and recall metrics. Finally, likelihood and sample quality can disagree: models with excellent NLL can produce poor samples, and models with great samples can assign high likelihood to out-of-distribution inputs, as documented for flows and VAEs.
ml-losses-04.further: Continue with normalizing flows and exact likelihood, score matching and the stochastic differential equation view of diffusion, flow matching and rectified flows, and classifier-free guidance. Study f-divergences and the variational bounds behind GAN variants, importance-weighted autoencoders, and vector-quantized VAEs that feed discrete tokens to autoregressive models. For language models, read about bits-per-byte evaluation, scaling laws for loss, and how the reverse-KL penalty in RLHF connects post-training back to the same divergence ideas.
